column3: The Hebrew says the LORD has “seen” a king for Himself among Jesse’s sons; BSB renders this as “selected.”
The Hebrew commands taking the heifer “in your hand”; BSB renders this as taking it “with you.”

The Hebrew leaves the one seeing Eliab unnamed; BSB supplies Samuel.
The Hebrew says a person sees “to the eyes,” retaining an eyes image; BSB renders this as seeing “the outward appearance.”
The Hebrew says Jesse made Abinadab pass before Samuel; BSB renders this movement as presenting him to Samuel.
The Hebrew says Jesse made Shammah pass and leaves the following speaker unnamed. BSB uses “presented” and explicitly identifies Samuel as the speaker.
The Hebrew explicitly names Jesse as the recipient of Samuel’s reply; BSB uses “him.”
The Hebrew has no separate verb corresponding to eating in “we will not sit down to eat.” BSB also identifies the respondent as Jesse, where the Hebrew leaves him unnamed.
The Hebrew says “he sent and brought him”; BSB supplies Jesse and “his youngest son.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the troubling spirit “evil”; BSB uses “a spirit of distress.” It has no separate verb meaning “began.”
The Hebrew calls it an “evil spirit of God”; BSB uses “a spirit of distress from God.”
The Hebrew calls the spirit “evil” and explicitly says the musician will play “with his hand”; BSB uses “of distress” and leaves the hand implicit.
The Hebrew introduces the words with “said” and includes a request particle; BSB specifies that Saul “commanded.”
The Hebrew says Jesse’s son knows how to play, without naming the instrument here; BSB supplies “the harp.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the gifts were sent “by the hand of David”; BSB renders this as “with his son David.”
The Hebrew says David stood before Saul and that Saul loved him greatly; BSB uses “entered his service” and “admired him greatly.”
The Hebrew asks that David “stand before me” and says he has “found favor in my eyes.” BSB renders these as remaining in Saul’s service and “I am pleased with him.”

The Hebrew separately describes relief for Saul and his becoming well, and explicitly mentions David playing with his hand. BSB combines the result as becoming well and leaves the hand implicit; it calls the evil spirit a “spirit of distress.”
